title: The Out-of-Range Price

scenario.situation: The demand model recommends a price 40% above anything seen in training data, projecting a 28% revenue lift. The optimizer says go.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The product team wants to trust the optimizer — it's the most sophisticated model the company has ever built, and the revenue projection looks compelling.
scenario.question: Should Priceright act on the optimizer's recommended price?

decisions.prompt: The product team is ready to ship the new price. How do you frame your investigation before signing off?

options.label: Validate the model's accuracy on held-out data
options.detail: Run standard holdout metrics (RMSE, R²) to confirm the model performs well.
options.consequence: The model scores well on held-out data — but that data came from the same observed price range as training. Good in-sample accuracy says nothing about what the model does outside that range. You've confirmed the wrong thing.
options.divergenceCost: Validated performance inside the training range, which doesn't speak to extrapolation risk.

options.label: Examine the model's predictions across the full price range, including unobserved territory
options.detail: Plot predicted demand vs. price from the lowest observed price through the recommended price — and flag where observed data ends.
options.consequence: You immediately see that the model's predicted demand curve continues near-linearly into a price region where Priceright has zero historical transactions. The recommendation lives entirely outside the training support. This is the thread everything else follows.

options.label: Benchmark the recommended price against competitors
options.detail: Check whether the new price is in line with market rates.
options.consequence: Competitor prices give context but don't tell you whether your model's demand curve is trustworthy at that price. You've added business color without touching the core reliability question.
options.divergenceCost: Shifted focus to external benchmarking and bypassed the model's structural limitation.

options.label: Ask the optimizer to generate a confidence interval around the projection
options.detail: Request uncertainty bands on the 28% revenue lift estimate.
options.consequence: The model produces confidence intervals — but they're computed from in-range variance and don't widen to reflect the total absence of data at the recommended price. The bands look reassuringly narrow and are structurally misleading.
options.divergenceCost: Relied on confidence intervals that don't account for out-of-support extrapolation.

decisions.prompt: You've plotted the model's predictions across the price range. Which metric best exposes whether the recommendation is trustworthy?

artifact.title: Predicted revenue lift by price point (model output)
artifact.caption: Projected revenue lift (%) climbs smoothly to the recommended price — but this is raw model output with no indication of where observed data ends.

options.label: Projected revenue lift from the model
options.detail: Use the optimizer's own revenue lift projections as the evidence of record.
options.consequence: The projections look smooth and compelling — they rise monotonically to the recommended price. But the model is generating these numbers by extrapolating a linear-ish trend, not from any observed demand signal. The chart is a picture of the model's assumptions, not reality.
options.divergenceCost: Treated model output as evidence without checking whether that output was grounded in data.

options.label: Density of observed transactions per price band
options.detail: Count how many real historical transactions fall within each $10 price band up to and including the recommended price.
options.consequence: The data density chart is stark: transaction counts are healthy through the current price range, drop sharply above $115, and hit zero by $125. The recommended price of $140 sits in a region with no observed support whatsoever. The model's confident projection is built on nothing.

artifact.title: Observed transaction density by price band
artifact.caption: Transaction count per price band. The recommended price falls in a band with zero observed transactions — the model has no real demand signal there.

decisions.prompt: The data shows the recommended price is entirely outside the model's training support. What do you tell the product team?

options.label: "The model is extrapolating — this price will collapse demand. Don't ship it."
options.detail: Make the definitive call that the recommended price is wrong.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified the extrapolation problem, but asserting that demand will collapse is itself an out-of-support claim — you don't actually have data there. The team may push back, and you have no empirical ground to stand on for the specific magnitude of harm.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed the outcome in the unobserved region rather than recommending a way to observe it.

options.label: "The projected lift is based on extrapolation with zero transaction support at that price — the model can't be trusted here. Let's constrain optimization to the observed range and run a limited price test to explore higher bands safely."
options.detail: Reframe the finding, flag the structural limit, and propose a path to real evidence.
options.consequence: You've shown the product team exactly where the model's knowledge ends, given them a safe interim recommendation (optimize within observed support), and proposed a price experiment that would generate real data — turning a risky ship into a structured learning opportunity.

insight: The optimizer's revenue projection was technically coherent — it was doing exactly what it was trained to do, fitting a curve and following it. The problem is that the curve ran off the edge of the data. Strong in-sample accuracy and smooth model output can mask the fact that a recommendation lives in a region the model has never seen. The lesson is structural: before acting on any model-driven optimum, check whether that optimum falls inside the observed support — and if it doesn't, the right move is a constrained recommendation plus an experiment, not a confident ship.
